summary:
Scotland forms part of the United Kingdom and its visitor-facing position rests on United Kingdom law; the material below is Scotland's own layer. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service reported 7,115 hate-crime charges for 2025-26, up 17% on the previous year and the highest annual total since 2003-04. Charges carrying a transgender-identity aggravation reached 104, a rise of 21% from 86 and the highest level since the 2021 Act took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category.

Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25 in the first annual report under the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021. Rates per 10,000 residents were highest in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each; 62% of recorded offences carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator. That publication gives no transgender-identity figure per head.

Scottish law attaches penalty enhancement to crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity under legislation enacted in 2009, and the hate-crime statute passed in March 2021 by 82-32, received royal assent a month later and took effect on 1 April 2024 with gender identity written in explicitly. A trans visitor therefore stands in a jurisdiction where identity-motivated hostility is an aggravating factor at charge and sentence.

Legal gender change in Scotland remains governed by the national Gender Recognition Act 2004. Scotland's own reform route did not reach the statute book: the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was introduced in March 2022 and passed by 86-39 that December, applying only to Scotland, then blocked by the United Kingdom government under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 while awaiting royal assent, the first use of that power against Scottish legislation. In 2018 the Scottish Government announced plans for an "X" sex descriptor on identity documents and a lower minimum transition age of 16.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, which passed on 4 February 2014 by 108-15 and received royal assent on 12 March 2014, with the first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to perform them. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under their current sex-marker status can marry in Scotland, and civil partnerships have been available since 2005.
tangentialFactors:
The charging figures are raw counts and neither publication supplies a population denominator for the transgender-identity category, so 104 charges cannot be expressed as a rate and the "highest since" comparison ranks raw totals across years rather than risk per head. Sexual-orientation charges at 2,062 outnumber them nearly twenty to one, while race carried 62% of police-recorded hate crimes.

The transgender-identity aggravation only exists under the 2021 Act, in force 1 April 2024, so no comparable series precedes it and the rise to 104 rests on a short run of years. Area-level comparison is possible on the police side, where Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh lead on recorded offences per 10,000 residents, but no equivalent area breakdown of transgender-identity charges is given.

Gender recognition is the sharpest point of friction between the Scottish Parliament and the United Kingdom government. The 2022 bill was stopped before assent through a section 35 order, a constitutional mechanism reserved to the national government, which leaves Scotland on the same national statutory footing as the rest of the United Kingdom rather than the self-identification route its own legislature voted for.
localsOnly:
Same-sex couples have held joint and stepchild adoption rights in Scotland since 28 September 2009, and the Looked After Children (Scotland) Regulations 2009 permit consideration as foster parents on the same basis as anyone else.

Civil partnerships have been available to same-sex couples in Scotland since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, conferring property, inheritance tax, social security, pension, parental responsibility, maintenance, tenancy, insurance and next-of-kin rights, with formal dissolution procedures akin to divorce.

Residents reporting hate crime deal with a system whose first full police-recording year under the 2021 Act produced 8,538 offences, and where the transgender-identity aggravator sits in the same chargeable machinery as the race and sexual-orientation aggravators.

For residents seeking to change legal gender, the section 35 block means the Scottish Parliament's intended route is unavailable and applications proceed under the national 2004 statute. The 2018 announcement of an "X" descriptor and a minimum transition age of 16 was a programme commitment, and this inventory records no implementing instrument behind it.
outOfScopeNotes:
The two hate-crime sources measure different things over different periods: the Crown Office counts charges for 2025-26 while the Scottish Government counts offences recorded by police for 2024-25. They are not a comparable series, and neither gives a per-capita rate for transgender-identity aggravation.

No prosecution or sentencing outcome data for the 104 transgender-identity charges appears in this inventory; whether those charges led to conviction is unresolved here.

The status of the 2018 "X" descriptor announcement, and whether the blocked Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was reintroduced or litigated after December 2022, is not sourced in this inventory.

Dates, vote counts and legislative history attributed in this inventory to a public encyclopedia entry have not been checked against the statutes themselves. The inventory also carries no Scotland-specific enforcement data on national equality or custody rules; those layers sit in the national record.
